translations.title: Costos Ocultos Al Importar: Los Cargos Que No Ves Venir
translations.excerpt: La cotización de importación casi nunca es el costo final. Estos son los cargos que aparecen después, por qué aparecen y qué puedes hacer para que no te sorprendan.
translations.content:
Los costos ocultos al importar a México son los cargos que no aparecen en la cotización inicial: almacenaje en recinto fiscal cuando la mercancía espera, maniobras de carga y descarga, reconocimiento aduanero si el semáforo sale rojo, rectificación de pedimento por un dato mal declarado, etiquetado NOM hecho en destino, y el IVA del 16 por ciento que inmoviliza tu efectivo aunque después lo acredites.

  • El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana a nivel nacional; es acreditable pero inmoviliza efectivo (SAT).
  • El DTA bajo T-MEC es una cuota fija de aproximadamente 362 MXN por pedimento; la prevalidación ronda 238 MXN (Ley Federal de Derechos).
  • El honorario del agente aduanal no está regulado: suele ir de 2,500 a 15,000 MXN, o de 0.35 a 0.65 por ciento del valor.
  • La mercancía de origen estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento de arancel bajo el T-MEC si tiene certificado de origen (SAT, USTR).
  • El almacenaje en recinto fiscal y las maniobras se cobran por tiempo y movimiento, así que una demora documental se convierte en dinero.

¿Qué costos ocultos aparecen al importar?

Almacenaje en recinto fiscal, maniobras, reconocimiento aduanero por semáforo rojo, rectificación de pedimento, etiquetado NOM hecho en México y el IVA que inmoviliza efectivo. Ninguno aparece en una cotización de flete, pero todos aparecen en la factura final.

Cuando pides una cotización para importar, casi siempre recibes dos números: el flete y el honorario del agente aduanal. El problema es que la operación real tiene más piezas, y las que faltan son justo las que se activan cuando algo no sale perfecto. El primer costo oculto es el almacenaje en recinto fiscal: mientras tu mercancía espera a que se resuelva un documento, el recinto cobra por día, y ese reloj corre aunque el retraso no sea tuyo. El segundo son las maniobras, es decir la carga, descarga y movimiento físico de la mercancía dentro del recinto, que se cobran por operación. El tercero es el reconocimiento aduanero: el semáforo fiscal puede salir rojo, la autoridad revisa físicamente la mercancía, y eso suma maniobras más uno o dos días de demora. El cuarto es la rectificación de pedimento, que ocurre cuando un dato quedó mal declarado y hay que corregirlo formalmente. El quinto es el etiquetado NOM: si tu producto llegó sin etiqueta en español, alguien tiene que ponerla en México, y ese trabajo se cobra por pieza. Y el sexto no es exactamente un cargo, pero pesa igual: el IVA de importación del 16 por ciento se paga al entrar, y aunque después lo acredites, mientras tanto es efectivo inmovilizado. Ninguno de estos aparece en la cotización inicial porque todos dependen de cómo salga la operación, no de la tarifa.

¿Cuánto cuesta cada concepto en la práctica?

El arancel de origen estadounidense es 0 por ciento con certificado T-MEC, el IVA 16 por ciento, el DTA una cuota fija cercana a 362 MXN y la prevalidación cerca de 238 MXN. El honorario del agente no está regulado y varía mucho, así que ahí es donde debes pedir el desglose.

Conviene separar los costos que están fijados por ley de los que dependen de quién te cotiza, porque solo los segundos se negocian. Del lado fijo, el IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana en todo el país, y el arancel para mercancía de origen estadounidense es 0 por ciento bajo el T-MEC siempre que exista certificado de origen, lo cual convierte ese documento en una de las piezas más rentables de la operación. El DTA, que es el derecho de trámite aduanero, bajo T-MEC es una cuota fija cercana a 362 MXN por pedimento en lugar del cálculo porcentual general, y la prevalidación ronda 238 MXN. Estas cifras se actualizan periódicamente, así que confírmalas con tu agente al momento de operar. Del lado variable está el honorario del agente aduanal, que no está regulado por ley: en el mercado suele ubicarse entre 2,500 y 15,000 MXN por pedimento, o bien entre 0.35 y 0.65 por ciento del valor de la mercancía, y esa horquilla es tan amplia porque incluye servicios distintos. Ahí es donde debes pedir el desglose por escrito. Los cargos por evento, como almacenaje, maniobras o reconocimiento, no tienen tarifa única porque dependen del recinto, del tiempo y del volumen, y por eso mismo no se pueden prometer en una cotización honesta. Lo que sí puede hacer un operador serio es decirte de antemano cuáles pueden activarse y en qué escenario.

¿Cómo evitas que te sorprendan?

Documentación impecable antes de que la mercancía llegue, clasificación arancelaria correcta, certificado de origen listo, etiqueta NOM puesta en origen y un solo responsable de toda la cadena. La mayoría de los costos ocultos no son tarifas: son consecuencias de un error o de una demora.

La buena noticia es que casi ningún costo oculto es inevitable, porque la mayoría no son tarifas sino consecuencias. Empieza por la documentación: factura, lista de empaque y valor declarado deben coincidir exactamente entre sí, porque la mayor parte de las demoras nace de que un documento dice algo distinto a otro. Sigue con la clasificación arancelaria, es decir la fracción con la que se declara tu producto, porque una fracción equivocada es la causa más común de rectificación de pedimento y también la que más riesgo de revisión genera. Prepara el certificado de origen antes de embarcar si tu mercancía es estadounidense, no después de que llegó. Etiqueta en origen: poner la etiqueta NOM en español antes de que la mercancía salga es siempre más barato que contratar a alguien para etiquetarla pieza por pieza en México, y además evita que la carga se detenga por incumplimiento. Consolida cuando puedas, porque los costos fijos como el pedimento, la prevalidación y el DTA se reparten entre más mercancía y el costo por unidad baja. Y sobre todo, trabaja con un solo responsable de la cadena completa: cuando el flete, el despacho y la entrega están en manos de empresas distintas, cada frontera entre ellas es un lugar donde el costo aparece y nadie lo asume. BringGo Ship opera con bodegas en Laredo y Monterrey y agente aduanal con patente propio, precisamente para que estos cargos se prevengan en lugar de explicarse después.

Definiciones

  • Recinto fiscal: El recinto fiscal es el área autorizada donde la mercancía permanece bajo control aduanero y donde se cobra almacenaje por el tiempo que espera.
  • Reconocimiento aduanero: El reconocimiento aduanero es la revisión física que hace la autoridad cuando el semáforo fiscal sale rojo, y añade maniobras y tiempo.
  • Rectificación de pedimento: La rectificación de pedimento es la corrección formal de un dato mal declarado, con costo y tiempo adicionales.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Qué costos ocultos aparecen al importar a México?

Almacenaje en recinto fiscal, maniobras, reconocimiento aduanero si el semáforo sale rojo, rectificación de pedimento, etiquetado NOM hecho en destino y el IVA del 16 por ciento que inmoviliza efectivo. No aparecen en la cotización porque dependen de cómo salga la operación, no de la tarifa.

¿Cuánto cobra un agente aduanal en México?

El honorario no está regulado por ley. En el mercado suele ubicarse entre 2,500 y 15,000 MXN por pedimento, o entre 0.35 y 0.65 por ciento del valor de la mercancía. La horquilla es amplia porque cada cotización incluye servicios distintos, así que pide el desglose por escrito antes de comparar.

¿El IVA de importación se recupera?

Sí, el IVA de importación del 16 por ciento es acreditable si estás dado de alta y cumples los requisitos fiscales. Pero se paga al momento de entrar la mercancía, así que entre el pago y la acreditación tu efectivo queda inmovilizado. Por eso conviene considerarlo en el flujo de caja aunque no sea un costo definitivo.

¿Cómo evito el almacenaje en aduana?

Teniendo la documentación completa y consistente antes de que la mercancía llegue. El almacenaje se cobra por día mientras la carga espera, y la mayoría de las esperas nacen de un documento que no coincide con otro o de una clasificación arancelaria equivocada. Preparar el expediente antes del embarque es lo que evita el reloj.

¿Consolidar reduce los costos ocultos?

Reduce los costos fijos por unidad, que es donde más se nota. El pedimento, la prevalidación y el DTA existen sin importar cuánta mercancía traes, así que juntar varios proveedores en una sola importación reparte esos montos entre más piezas. Además reduce el número de operaciones y con ello las oportunidades de error.

translations.title: Lo Que Nadie Te Dice Antes De Importar A México: 12 Verdades
translations.excerpt: Antes de tu primera importación a México hay una docena de cosas que casi nadie te explica y que definen si la operación sale bien. Aquí están, sin adorno.
translations.content:
Antes de importar a México necesitas saber que hace falta estar inscrito en el padrón de importadores, que solo un agente aduanal con patente puede presentar el pedimento, que la fracción arancelaria define tu impuesto y tu riesgo, que la etiqueta en español es obligatoria antes de que la mercancía entre, y que el IVA del 16 por ciento se paga al ingresar aunque después lo acredites.

  • Solo un agente aduanal con patente puede presentar el pedimento que legaliza la importación (SAT).
  • La inscripción en el padrón de importadores es requisito para importar de forma regular (SAT).
  • La etiqueta en español conforme a la NOM aplicable es obligatoria para la mayoría del retail (NOM-050, NOM-051 y sectoriales).
  • El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana; es acreditable pero se paga al entrar (SAT).
  • La mercancía de origen estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento de arancel bajo T-MEC con certificado de origen (USTR, SAT).

¿Qué debería saber antes de mi primera importación?

Que la importación es un trámite legal, no solo un envío. Necesitas estar en el padrón de importadores, trabajar con un agente aduanal con patente, clasificar bien tu producto y tener la etiqueta en español lista. Sin estas cuatro piezas, la mercancía se detiene.

La primera verdad es la más incómoda: importar no es enviar. Un envío se contrata y se rastrea, pero una importación es un acto legal en el que alguien declara ante la autoridad qué entra al país, de dónde viene y cuánto vale, y asume la responsabilidad de que eso sea cierto. De ahí nacen las cuatro piezas que casi nadie menciona en la primera llamada. Uno, necesitas estar inscrito en el padrón de importadores para importar de forma regular, y ese registro toma tiempo, así que no se resuelve el día que llega la mercancía. Dos, solo un agente aduanal con patente puede presentar el pedimento, que es el documento que legaliza la operación; no lo puede hacer tu transportista ni tú. Tres, tu producto debe estar clasificado en una fracción arancelaria correcta, porque de esa fracción dependen el impuesto que pagas y las regulaciones que te aplican, y una clasificación mal hecha es la causa más común de problemas posteriores. Y cuatro, la etiqueta en español conforme a la norma aplicable tiene que existir antes de que la mercancía entre, no después de que la tengas en tu bodega. Si estas cuatro piezas están listas, la importación es rutina. Si falta una, la mercancía espera, y en aduana esperar cuesta dinero todos los días.

Las verdades sobre el dinero

El arancel no es tu mayor costo, el IVA sí pesa en el flujo. El origen estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento bajo T-MEC pero solo con certificado. Los costos fijos hacen que importar poco salga caro por unidad, y la cotización más barata suele ser la que menos incluye.

La quinta verdad es que el arancel casi nunca es tu mayor costo, y eso sorprende a casi todos. Si tu mercancía es de origen estadounidense y tienes certificado de origen, entra con 0 por ciento de arancel bajo el T-MEC, así que el impuesto que sí vas a pagar siempre es el IVA del 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana. La sexta es que ese IVA es acreditable, pero se paga al entrar, de modo que entre el desembolso y la acreditación hay un hueco de flujo de caja que conviene planear. La séptima es que el certificado de origen no se emite solo: alguien tiene que prepararlo, y si nadie lo hace, pagas arancel por una mercancía que tenía derecho a no pagarlo. La octava es que los costos fijos de una importación existen sin importar el volumen. El pedimento, la prevalidación y el derecho de trámite se pagan igual traigas una tarima o veinte, así que importar cantidades pequeñas siempre sale caro por unidad, y por eso la consolidación es la palanca de costo más grande que tiene un importador nuevo. La novena es que la cotización más barata normalmente es la que menos incluye: si un precio parece la mitad que los demás, casi siempre es porque el despacho, el etiquetado o la entrega nacional están fuera. Pide siempre el desglose y compara conceptos, no totales.

Las verdades sobre el tiempo y el riesgo

El semáforo fiscal puede salir rojo y añadir días, la mayoría de las demoras vienen de documentos que no coinciden, y las devoluciones se planean antes de la primera venta. Un solo responsable de la cadena elimina los puntos donde la carga se queda esperando.

La décima verdad es que el tiempo en frontera no depende de la distancia sino del papeleo. Laredo y Monterrey están a unas horas de camino, y una carga bien documentada cruza y se entrega en uno a dos días hábiles, pero un documento inconsistente puede sumar días completos, así que la calidad del expediente vale más que la velocidad del camión. La undécima es el semáforo fiscal: al presentar el pedimento, el sistema puede marcar reconocimiento aduanero, y entonces la autoridad revisa físicamente la mercancía. No es un castigo ni implica que hiciste algo mal, pero suma maniobras y tiempo, y por eso ninguna operación seria promete una fecha exacta de entrega sin margen. La duodécima, y la que más caro sale ignorar, es que las devoluciones se diseñan antes de la primera venta. Si vendes en México y tu única dirección de retorno está en Estados Unidos, cada devolución se convierte en una exportación con su propio costo y su propio trámite, y el cliente mexicano espera devolver como devuelve en cualquier tienda local. Tener un punto de retorno nacional cambia por completo esa ecuación. Estas doce verdades tienen un hilo común: casi ningún problema de importación es un problema de transporte, son problemas de preparación. Por eso conviene trabajar con un operador que controle toda la cadena. BringGo Ship opera bodegas en Laredo y Monterrey con agente aduanal con patente propio, para que la preparación pase antes de que la mercancía se mueva.

Definiciones

  • Pedimento: El pedimento es el documento aduanero que legaliza la importación y que solo puede presentar un agente aduanal con patente.
  • Padrón de importadores: El padrón de importadores es el registro ante el SAT que habilita a una empresa a importar de forma regular.
  • Semáforo fiscal: El semáforo fiscal determina si la mercancía se libera directamente o pasa a reconocimiento aduanero para revisión física.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Qué debería saber antes de mi primera importación a México?

Que importar es un trámite legal, no solo un envío. Necesitas estar inscrito en el padrón de importadores, trabajar con un agente aduanal con patente, clasificar correctamente tu producto en una fracción arancelaria y tener la etiqueta en español lista antes de que la mercancía entre. Sin esas cuatro piezas, la carga se detiene.

¿Puedo importar sin agente aduanal?

No para una operación comercial regular. El pedimento que legaliza la importación solo lo puede presentar un agente aduanal con patente, así que ese paso no se puede saltar ni delegar en el transportista. Existen esquemas simplificados para envíos pequeños por mensajería, pero no sustituyen al despacho formal cuando importas para vender.

¿Cuál es el mayor costo al importar?

Normalmente no es el arancel. La mercancía de origen estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento bajo el T-MEC si tiene certificado de origen, así que el impuesto real es el IVA del 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana. A eso se suman los costos fijos por pedimento, que son los que encarecen las importaciones pequeñas.

¿Por qué mi mercancía se queda detenida en aduana?

Casi siempre por documentos que no coinciden entre sí, por una fracción arancelaria equivocada o por falta de etiqueta en español. También puede tocar reconocimiento aduanero si el semáforo sale rojo, lo cual añade maniobras y tiempo sin que hayas hecho nada mal. La prevención está en el expediente, no en el camión.

¿Cuándo debo pensar en las devoluciones?

Antes de tu primera venta. Si vendes en México y tu única dirección de retorno está en Estados Unidos, cada devolución se convierte en una exportación con costo y trámite propios. Un punto de retorno nacional permite recibir, revisar y volver a poner a la venta sin cruzar la frontera cada vez.

translations.title: El Modelo Híbrido: Dropshipping Con Inventario En La Frontera
translations.excerpt: El dropshipping puro es barato pero lento; el inventario propio es rápido pero caro. El modelo híbrido, con un stock pequeño en la frontera, te da lo mejor de ambos.
translations.content:
El modelo híbrido consiste en mantener un stock pequeño de tus productos más vendidos en una bodega fronteriza mientras el resto del catálogo sigue en dropshipping. Los productos con rotación se reponen a México en uno o dos días y se entregan como envío nacional, y los productos de baja rotación no inmovilizan capital porque solo se piden cuando alguien los compra.

  • En dropshipping puro cada paquete cruza la frontera por separado y paga trámite aduanero por envío.
  • Consolidar un stock pequeño en la frontera reparte el costo fijo del pedimento entre muchas unidades.
  • Una carga bien documentada llega de Laredo a Monterrey en uno a dos días hábiles (dato operativo).
  • Desde bodega en México la entrega es nacional, no una importación por pedido.
  • El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana sin importar el modelo elegido (SAT).

¿Cómo acelero mi dropshipping con una bodega fronteriza?

Manteniendo en la frontera solo los productos que más vendes y dejando el resto en dropshipping. Los que tienen rotación se reponen a México en uno o dos días y se entregan como envío nacional; los que casi no se venden no inmovilizan tu capital.

El dropshipping puro tiene una ventaja enorme y una debilidad enorme, y el modelo híbrido existe para conservar la primera sin cargar con la segunda. La ventaja es que no inmovilizas capital: solo compras cuando alguien ya te compró. La debilidad es el tiempo, porque cada pedido viaja como un envío internacional independiente y cada paquete pasa por trámite aduanero por separado, así que el cliente mexicano espera más de lo que espera en cualquier tienda local. El modelo híbrido resuelve esto sin obligarte a comprar inventario completo. La idea es simple: identifica los productos que concentran la mayor parte de tus ventas, que en casi cualquier catálogo son pocos, y mantén de ellos un stock pequeño en una bodega fronteriza. El resto del catálogo, la cola larga que se vende de vez en cuando, sigue exactamente como antes en dropshipping. Cuando alguien compra uno de tus productos estrella, sale de la bodega y se entrega como envío nacional, no como importación. Cuando compra algo raro, se pide como siempre. El resultado es que la mayoría de tus pedidos, que son los de los productos con rotación, se entregan rápido, mientras que tu capital sigue sin quedarse atrapado en las referencias que no giran. Es una decisión de portafolio, no de todo o nada.

¿Por qué la frontera y no una bodega en el centro del país?

Porque en la frontera puedes consolidar mercancía de varios proveedores en una sola importación, repartir el costo fijo del pedimento y reponer a México en uno o dos días. Es el punto donde el inventario está cerca del cliente sin haber entrado todavía al país.

La ubicación no es un detalle, es lo que hace que el modelo funcione económicamente. Una bodega en la frontera cumple dos funciones al mismo tiempo. La primera es la consolidación: puedes recibir mercancía de varios proveedores, juntarla y hacer una sola importación en lugar de muchas pequeñas. Esto importa porque los costos fijos de una importación, como el pedimento, la prevalidación y el derecho de trámite, se pagan igual traigas poco o mucho, así que repartirlos entre más unidades es la palanca que baja tu costo por producto. La segunda función es la proximidad: desde la frontera la reposición hacia el mercado mexicano es corta, y una carga bien documentada llega de Laredo a Monterrey en uno o dos días hábiles. Eso permite que tu stock en México sea pequeño, porque puedes reponerlo rápido en lugar de acumular meses de inventario por miedo a quedarte sin producto. Una bodega en el centro del país te da cercanía pero no te da consolidación, porque para llegar ahí la mercancía ya tuvo que importarse. Una bodega solo en Estados Unidos te da consolidación pero deja cada pedido cruzando la frontera individualmente. La frontera es el punto donde tienes las dos cosas: mercancía agrupada, lista, y a dos días del cliente. Sobre esa base es donde el híbrido deja de ser una idea y se vuelve una operación.

¿Cómo lo montas en la práctica?

Identifica el veinte por ciento de productos que hace la mayoría de tus ventas, calcula cuántas semanas de venta quieres tener disponibles, etiqueta en origen conforme a la NOM y define quién repone. Empieza pequeño y amplía según los datos, no según la intuición.

Montar el modelo híbrido es un ejercicio de datos, y se puede empezar con muy poco. Primer paso: mira tus ventas de los últimos meses y ordena tus productos por unidades vendidas. En casi todos los catálogos una minoría de referencias concentra la mayoría de los pedidos, y esas son las únicas que necesitan stock adelantado. Segundo paso: decide cuántas semanas de venta quieres tener disponibles. Como la reposición desde la frontera es corta, no necesitas meses; unas pocas semanas suelen bastar y eso mantiene bajo el capital comprometido. Tercer paso: etiqueta en origen. Tu producto necesita etiqueta en español conforme a la norma aplicable para entrar y para venderse, y ponerla antes de embarcar siempre es más barato que hacerlo pieza por pieza en destino. Cuarto paso: define quién repone y con qué señal. Lo más simple es fijar un punto de reorden por producto, de modo que cuando el stock baja de cierto nivel se dispara la siguiente consolidación sin que nadie tenga que acordarse. Quinto paso: mide. Compara el tiempo de entrega y la tasa de cancelación de los productos con stock contra los que siguen en dropshipping, porque esa diferencia es la que te dice si conviene mover más referencias al stock o no. Empieza con pocas referencias y crece con evidencia. BringGo Ship opera bodegas en Laredo y Monterrey con agente aduanal con patente propio, así que la consolidación, el etiquetado, el despacho y la entrega nacional quedan en una sola cadena.

Dropshipping puro vs híbrido vs inventario completo

FactorDropshipping puroModelo híbrido
Capital inmovilizadoNingunoBajo, solo los que giran
AduanaPor cada paqueteConsolidada, por lote
Entrega al clienteEnvío internacionalEnvío nacional
Costo por unidadAlto en volumenBaja al consolidar
Cola larga del catálogoIdealSe queda en dropshipping

Definiciones

  • Modelo híbrido: El modelo híbrido mantiene stock adelantado solo de los productos de alta rotación y deja el resto del catálogo en dropshipping.
  • Stock buffer: El stock buffer es la cantidad pequeña de inventario que se mantiene adelantada para cubrir la venta mientras llega la siguiente reposición.
  • Punto de reorden: El punto de reorden es el nivel de inventario que dispara automáticamente la siguiente reposición sin decisión manual.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Cómo acelero mi dropshipping hacia México?

Manteniendo un stock pequeño de tus productos más vendidos en una bodega fronteriza y dejando el resto del catálogo en dropshipping. Los productos con rotación se reponen a México en uno o dos días y se entregan como envío nacional, mientras que los de baja rotación no inmovilizan capital porque solo se piden cuando alguien los compra.

¿Cuánto inventario necesito para el modelo híbrido?

Menos del que crees, porque la reposición desde la frontera es corta. Suele bastar con unas pocas semanas de venta de tus referencias de mayor rotación, en lugar de meses de inventario. La idea es cubrir el tiempo de reposición, no acumular stock por precaución.

¿Por qué una bodega en la frontera y no dentro de México?

Porque en la frontera puedes consolidar mercancía de varios proveedores en una sola importación y repartir el costo fijo del pedimento entre más unidades. Una bodega ya dentro de México te da cercanía pero no consolidación, porque para llegar ahí la mercancía ya se importó pieza por pieza.

¿El modelo híbrido reduce los impuestos?

No reduce las tasas. El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana con cualquier modelo, y el arancel depende del origen de la mercancía. Lo que reduce es el costo logístico por unidad, porque consolidar reparte los costos fijos de la importación entre mucha más mercancía.

¿Qué productos debo mantener en stock?

Los que concentran la mayoría de tus pedidos, que en casi cualquier catálogo son pocas referencias. Ordena tus ventas por unidades y empieza solo con las de arriba. Las referencias que se venden de vez en cuando conviene dejarlas en dropshipping, porque ahí el capital inmovilizado no se justifica.

Monta tu stock en la frontera con BringGo Ship

translations.title: Setting Up A Local Return Address In Mexico: Why It Changes Everything
translations.excerpt: If your only return address is in the US, every Mexican return becomes an export. A local return point turns it into a domestic parcel and changes your economics.
translations.content:
A local return address in Mexico is a domestic address where your Mexican customers send returns, instead of shipping them back across the border. It turns each return from a small export with its own paperwork into an ordinary domestic parcel, which cuts the cost per return, shortens refund time, and lets good units go straight back into sellable inventory inside Mexico.

  • Without a local address, every return crosses the border individually and carries its own formalities.
  • A domestic return parcel inside Mexico typically moves in a normal local carrier window, not an international one.
  • Returned units that pass inspection can be restocked in Mexico instead of being re-imported later.
  • Only units genuinely worth recovering need to travel back to the US, and they can move consolidated.
  • Mexican consumer protection rules give buyers warranty and return rights, so returns are a cost of selling, not an exception (PROFECO).

Why does a local Mexican return address cut costs and refund times?

Because it removes the border from the return trip. A return to a domestic address is an ordinary parcel; a return to the US is a small export with paperwork, cost and delay attached to a single item. The first is routine, the second is expensive every single time.

The economics of returns break at the border, and a local address is what stops that from happening. When your only return address is in the United States, a customer in Guadalajara who wants to send back one pair of shoes is starting an international shipment. That single item needs a carrier that handles cross-border parcels, it needs documentation, and it moves at international speed rather than domestic speed. Everything about that trip is disproportionate to the value of the item inside it, and you pay that disproportion on every return you accept. When the return address is inside Mexico, the same shoes become an ordinary domestic parcel. The customer drops it off the way they would with any local store, it arrives in a normal local delivery window, and your team inspects it days sooner. That speed matters for more than convenience: the faster you confirm the item came back, the faster you can issue the refund, and refund speed is one of the things shoppers judge a store on. There is also a second saving that most sellers miss. A unit that comes back in good condition and is already inside Mexico can go straight back into sellable stock. If that same unit had traveled to the US, you would eventually pay to import it again in order to sell it to the next Mexican customer, paying twice to move one product in a circle.

What actually happens to a returned unit?

It arrives at your Mexican return point, gets inspected and graded, and then follows one of three paths: back into sellable stock, into a discounted or refurbished channel, or into disposal. Only genuinely valuable units are worth sending back to the US, and those travel consolidated.

A return address on its own is only a mailbox; what makes it useful is the process behind it. When a parcel arrives at your Mexican return point, the first step is intake, which means logging what came back and against which order, because a return you cannot match to an order is a refund dispute waiting to happen. The second step is inspection and grading, where each unit is sorted honestly into condition tiers rather than treated as a single pile. From there each unit takes one of three paths. Units in resellable condition go straight back into your Mexican inventory, and this is where the model pays for itself, because that unit becomes revenue again without crossing any border. Units with light damage or opened packaging go into a secondary path, which might mean a discounted listing, refurbishment, or a bundle, depending on what your category allows. Units that are genuinely unsellable go to disposal, and it is worth being decisive here, because storing worthless inventory costs more than writing it off. Only after that sorting does the question of sending anything north make sense. Usually the answer is that a small minority of items justify the trip, and when they do, they should travel together as one consolidated shipment rather than one by one. That single decision, sorting first and shipping consolidated second, is what separates a return process that controls cost from one that quietly bleeds it.

How do you set one up?

Decide who receives, publish clear return instructions in Spanish, define your inspection and grading rules, and agree what happens to each grade. Most sellers use a fulfillment partner already inside Mexico rather than opening their own facility, because returns volume rarely justifies a lease.

Setting up a local return address is less about real estate than about deciding who does the work. The first decision is who receives the returns. Very few sellers need their own Mexican facility for this, because returns volume is usually a fraction of outbound volume and a lease plus staff is hard to justify. In practice most sellers use a fulfillment partner that already operates inside Mexico, which gives them a real domestic address, a team to inspect, and a place to hold restocked units. The second decision is what the customer sees. Your return instructions need to be in Spanish, easy to find, and specific about the window, the condition expected, and how the refund is issued, because vague return policies generate support tickets and chargebacks rather than returns. Remember that Mexican consumer protection rules give buyers warranty and return rights, so the policy you publish has to sit comfortably inside those rules rather than pretend they do not exist. The third decision is the grading rulebook. Write down, before the first return arrives, what counts as resellable, what goes to a secondary channel, and what gets disposed of, so that the decision is consistent and does not depend on who opened the box. The fourth is the exception path, meaning what happens to the small number of items worth repatriating and how often those consolidate. Once these four are written down, the return address stops being a cost center and becomes a recovery channel. BringGo Ship runs warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey, so a Mexican return point, inspection, restocking and consolidated northbound returns sit in one chain.

Return to the US vs return to a Mexican address

FactorUS-only return addressLocal Mexican address
What the trip isSmall export, per itemOrdinary domestic parcel
Customer experienceInternational, unfamiliarLike any local store
Refund timingWaits on the borderDays sooner
Resellable unitsMust be re-importedRestocked in Mexico
Northbound shippingEvery itemOnly what is worth it, consolidated

Definitions

  • Local return address: A local return address is a domestic Mexican address where customers send returns, so the parcel never crosses the border.
  • Grading: Grading is sorting returned units by condition so each one follows the right path: restock, secondary channel or disposal.
  • Consolidated return: A consolidated return groups the few items worth sending back to the US into a single shipment instead of many individual ones.

Frequently asked questions

Why does a local Mexican return address cut costs and refund times?

Because it takes the border out of the return trip. A return to a domestic address is an ordinary parcel that moves in a local delivery window; a return to the US is a small export with paperwork and international timing attached to a single item. Faster arrival also means you can confirm and refund sooner.

Do I need my own warehouse in Mexico for returns?

Usually not. Returns volume is normally a fraction of outbound volume, so a lease and staff are hard to justify. Most sellers use a fulfillment partner already operating inside Mexico, which provides a genuine domestic address, a team to inspect and grade units, and space to hold anything that goes back into sellable stock.

What happens to items that come back in good condition?

They go straight back into your Mexican inventory and can be sold to the next customer without crossing any border. This is where the model pays for itself. If that unit had traveled back to the US instead, you would eventually pay to import it again to sell it in Mexico, paying twice to move one product in a circle.

Should I ever ship returns back to the US?

Only for the minority of items where the recovered value clearly justifies the trip, and when you do, send them together as one consolidated shipment rather than one at a time. Sorting first and shipping consolidated second is what keeps a returns process from quietly bleeding money.

What do Mexican return rules require of me?

Mexican consumer protection rules give buyers warranty and return rights, so returns are a normal cost of selling rather than an exception you can refuse. Publish your return policy in Spanish, be specific about the window and the condition expected, and make sure what you publish sits comfortably inside those rules.

  • SAT (Mexican tax administration) (sat.gob.mx)
  • USTR, USMCA (ustr.gov)

translations.title: FBA Meksika'ya Gönderim Maliyet Kalemleri: Eksiksiz Liste
translations.excerpt: Amazon Meksika FBA'de ödeyeceğin kalemler ürün fiyatından çok daha fazlası. Abonelikten stopaja kadar hepsini, doğrulanmış 2026 rakamlarıyla sıraladık.
translations.content:
Amazon Meksika FBA'de beş ana kalem var: profesyonel satıcı aboneliği (yeni satıcıda 12 ay ücretsiz, sonra aylık satışa göre 75 veya 600 MXN), kategori komisyonu (yüzde 8 ila 20, asgari 8 MXN), FBA gönderi işleme ücreti, depolama ücreti (dm3 başına, son çeyrekte artıyor) ve vergi stopajı. RFC'si olmayan yabancı satıcıda stopaj toplam yüzde 36'ya çıkıyor.

  • Profesyonel abonelik kademeli: yeni satıcı 12 ay ücretsiz, sonra önceki ay satışı 26.000 MXN altındaysa 75 MXN, üstündeyse 600 MXN (Amazon México).
  • Kategori komisyonu yüzde 8 ila 20, her kategoride asgari 8,00 MXN, ve toplam satış fiyatı üzerinden hesaplanıyor (Amazon México).
  • FBA gönderi ücreti boyut, ağırlık ve ürün fiyat bandının üçlü çarpımı; 299 MXN eşiğinde ücret belirgin şekilde düşüyor (Amazon México, 4 Haziran 2026 tarifesi).
  • Depolama dm3 başına: Ocak-Eylül 0,36 MXN, Ekim-Aralık 0,53 MXN (standart boyut); uzun dönem cezası 181. günde başlıyor (Amazon México).
  • RFC'si olmayan satıcıdan yüzde 16 IVA ve yüzde 20 ISR stopajı kesiliyor; RFC'li ve Meksika banka hesaplı satıcıda bu oran yüzde 8 ve yüzde 2,5'e iniyor (LISR 113-B, doğrula).

FBA gönderiminde hangi kalemler var?

Beş ana kalem: profesyonel abonelik, kategori komisyonu, FBA gönderi işleme ücreti, depolama ücreti ve vergi stopajı. Buna bir de Meksika'ya sokmanın maliyeti ekleniyor: gümrük müşaviri, yüzde 16 IVA ve İspanyolca NOM etiketi.

Amazon Meksika'da FBA ile satarken ödediğin şey tek bir komisyon değil, üst üste binen beş ayrı kalem, ve bunların üstüne bir de malı Meksika'ya sokmanın maliyeti geliyor. Birinci kalem profesyonel satıcı aboneliği. Bu artık sabit değil, kademeli: yeni satıcılar ilk 12 ay ücretsiz, sonrasında önceki ayki satışın 26.000 MXN'nin altındaysa ayda 75 MXN, üstündeyse ayda 600 MXN ödüyorsun. Meksika, ABD ve Kanada'yı birleşik hesapla yönetiyorsan aylık 39,99 USD tek ücret geçerli. İkinci kalem kategori komisyonu, yani referral. Kategoriye göre yüzde 8 ila 20 arasında değişiyor ve her kategoride asgari 8,00 MXN var. Buradaki en çok atlanan detay şu: komisyon sadece ürün fiyatı üzerinden değil, kargo ve hediye paketi dahil toplam satış fiyatı üzerinden hesaplanıyor. Üçüncü kalem FBA gönderi işleme ücreti, dördüncü kalem depolama, beşinci kalem ise vergi stopajı, ki bu sonuncusu yabancı satıcıda en pahalı sürprizdir. Bunların hepsinin dışında, mal Meksika'ya girerken gümrük müşaviri ücreti, yüzde 16 IVA ve İspanyolca NOM etiketi maliyeti var. Yani FBA ücretlerini hesaplarken sadece Amazon tarafına bakmak, tablonun yarısını görmek demek.

En çok atlanan ayrıntı: 299 MXN eşiği

FBA gönderi ücreti sadece boyut ve ağırlığa göre değil, ürünün fiyat bandına göre de değişiyor. Aynı fiziksel ürünün fiyatı 299 MXN'nin altına indiğinde gönderi ücreti belirgin şekilde düşüyor, yani Meksika'da fiyatlandırma ile lojistik maliyeti birbirine kilitli.

Meksika'nın FBA ücret yapısının ABD'den en önemli farkı burada ve çoğu satıcı bunu geç fark ediyor. Ücret, boyut kademesi, gönderi ağırlığı ve ürünün fiyat bandının üçlü çarpımıyla belirleniyor. Dört fiyat bandı var: 150 MXN altı, 150 ila 299, 299 ila 499 ve 499 üstü. Aynı fiziksel ürün, sadece fiyatı değiştiği için farklı gönderi ücreti ödüyor. Örnek olarak, 4 Haziran 2026 tarifesine göre standart boyutta 1 kilogramın üzerindeki bir ürün, fiyatı 499 MXN üstündeyse 72,80 MXN gönderi ücreti öderken, aynı ürün 150 MXN altında fiyatlandığında 28,50 MXN ödüyor. Bu, fiyatı 299 MXN eşiğinin hemen üstünde olan ürünlerde çok kritik bir karar noktası yaratıyor: fiyatı bir miktar düşürmek, komisyon kaybını gönderi ücretindeki düşüşle fazlasıyla telafi edebiliyor. Ayrıca ağırlık hesabında birim ağırlık ile hacimsel ağırlıktan hangisi büyükse o kullanılıyor, ambalaj ağırlığı ise artık sayılmıyor, dolayısıyla hafif ama hacimli ürünlerde ambalajı küçültmek doğrudan ücreti düşürüyor. Gıda, sağlık ve kişisel bakım kategorilerinde ayrı ve çok daha ucuz bir tarife var; standart boyutta 150 MXN altı üründe gönderi ücreti 5,00 MXN'e kadar inebiliyor. Bu rakamlar Amazon tarafından güncelleniyor, o yüzden bütçeni yaparken Seller Central'daki güncel tabloyu esas al.

Depolama, uzun dönem cezası ve stopaj

Depolama dm3 başına ve son çeyrekte artıyor. Uzun dönem cezası 181. günde başlıyor, 365'te değil. En pahalı kalem ise stopaj: RFC'si olmayan yabancı satıcı, para eline geçmeden cironun yüzde 36'sını kaybediyor.

Depolama ücreti metreküp değil desimetreküp üzerinden hesaplanıyor ve mevsimsel. Standart boyutta Ocak-Eylül arası dm3 başına 0,36 MXN iken, Ekim-Aralık arasında 0,53 MXN'e çıkıyor; büyük boyutta bu fark daha da sert, 0,19'dan 0,43 MXN'e yükseliyor. Yani yılbaşı sezonuna erken ve fazla stok göndermek, ürünü satmadan önce depolama faturasını büyütüyor. Uzun dönem depolama cezası konusunda dolaşımdaki bilgi genelde yanlış: ceza 365 günde değil, 181. günde başlıyor ve kademeli olarak artıyor, bir yılı geçen envanterde dm3 başına 4,76 MXN veya birim başına 2,32 MXN gibi ciddi bir seviyeye ulaşıyor. Envanteri kaldırmak veya imha etmek de ücretli, birim başına ortalama 10,70 ve 13,00 MXN civarında. Ama yabancı satıcı için en pahalı kalem bunların hiçbiri değil, stopaj. Amazon Meksika'da satan ve RFC'si bulunmayan bir satıcıdan yüzde 16 IVA ve yüzde 20 ISR kesiliyor; yani ciron daha eline geçmeden yüzde 36'sı gidiyor, üstüne kategori komisyonu ve FBA ücreti biniyor. RFC'si olan ve Meksika banka hesabı kullanan satıcıda bu oranlar yüzde 8 IVA ve yüzde 2,5 ISR'ye iniyor. Aradaki fark o kadar büyük ki, Meksika'da vergi kaydı olmadan FBA yapmak çoğu üründe kârı tamamen siliyor. Bu oranların ondalıklarını Seller Central'dan ve mali müşavirinden mutlaka teyit et; yön ve büyüklük nettir ama mevzuat 2026'da güncellendi. BringGo Ship, Laredo ve Monterrey depoları ve lisanslı gümrük müşaviriyle malı Meksika'ya sokma tarafını yönetiyor, böylece Amazon tarafındaki kalemler senin tek odağın oluyor.

Kategori komisyonu%8-20, asgari 8 MXNToplam satış fiyatı üzerinden
FBA gönderi ücretiboyut x ağırlık x fiyat bandı299 MXN eşiği belirleyici
Depolama (standart)0,36 MXN/dm3Ekim-Aralık 0,53 MXN
Uzun dönem cezası181. günde başlar365 değil
Stopaj (RFC yoksa)%16 IVA + %20 ISRRFC varsa %8 + %2,5

Tanımlar

  • Referral (kategori komisyonu): Referral, Amazon'un her satıştan aldığı kategori komisyonudur ve ürün fiyatı ile kargo dahil toplam satış tutarı üzerinden hesaplanır.
  • Fiyat bandı: Fiyat bandı, Meksika FBA'de gönderi ücretini belirleyen dört ürün fiyatı aralığıdır ve aynı ürünün ücretini fiyatına göre değiştirir.
  • Stopaj (retención): Stopaj, Amazon'un satıcıya ödeme yapmadan önce kestiği IVA ve ISR tutarıdır ve RFC durumuna göre ciddi biçimde değişir.

Sık sorulan sorular

Amazon Meksika FBA'de hangi maliyet kalemleri var?

Beş ana kalem var: profesyonel abonelik (yeni satıcıda 12 ay ücretsiz, sonra 75 veya 600 MXN), kategori komisyonu (yüzde 8-20, asgari 8 MXN), FBA gönderi işleme ücreti, depolama ücreti ve vergi stopajı. Bunlara ek olarak malı Meksika'ya sokmanın maliyeti var: gümrük müşaviri, yüzde 16 IVA ve İspanyolca NOM etiketi.

Amazon Meksika aboneliği ne kadar?

Artık kademeli. Yeni satıcılar ilk 12 ay ücretsiz kullanıyor. Sonrasında önceki ayki satışın 26.000 MXN'nin altındaysa ayda 75 MXN, üstündeyse ayda 600 MXN ödüyorsun. Meksika, ABD ve Kanada'yı birleşik hesapla yönetiyorsan aylık 39,99 USD tek ücret geçerli.

FBA gönderi ücreti neye göre değişiyor?

Boyut kademesi, gönderi ağırlığı ve ürünün fiyat bandının üçlü çarpımına göre. Dört fiyat bandı var ve 299 MXN eşiği kritik: aynı fiziksel ürün, fiyatı düştüğünde belirgin şekilde daha düşük gönderi ücreti ödüyor. Ağırlıkta birim ile hacimsel ağırlıktan büyük olan kullanılıyor, ambalaj ağırlığı sayılmıyor.

Amazon Meksika depolama ücreti ne kadar?

Desimetreküp başına hesaplanıyor ve mevsimsel. Standart boyutta Ocak-Eylül arası 0,36 MXN, Ekim-Aralık arası 0,53 MXN. Büyük boyutta 0,19'dan 0,43 MXN'e çıkıyor. Yani yılbaşı sezonuna çok erken ve fazla stok göndermek, satış olmadan depolama faturasını büyütüyor.

RFC olmadan Amazon Meksika'da satılır mı?

Satılır ama çok pahalıya. RFC'si olmayan satıcıdan yüzde 16 IVA ve yüzde 20 ISR stopajı kesiliyor, yani ciron eline geçmeden yüzde 36'sı gidiyor. RFC'li ve Meksika banka hesaplı satıcıda bu oranlar yüzde 8 ve yüzde 2,5'e iniyor. Aradaki fark çoğu üründe kârın tamamını belirliyor, o yüzden bu kararı mali müşavirinle konuş.

translations.title: Mexican Consumer Trust: Reviews, Invoices And Signals That Convert
translations.excerpt: Mexican shoppers abandon carts for specific, documented reasons, and two of the top five are things a cross-border seller controls. Here is what the data actually says.
translations.content:
Mexican shoppers trust an online store when the shipping cost is visible early, the site looks and feels legitimate, their preferred payment method is accepted, and the return policy is clear. Those are four of the five reasons AMVO records for abandoned purchases. Mexican law adds a hard requirement: you must publish a physical address and phone number before the transaction.

  • Mexican e-commerce reached 941 billion MXN in 2025, growing 19.2 percent year over year with 77.2 million online buyers (AMVO).
  • Online now accounts for 17.7 percent of Mexican retail, and e-commerce grew roughly 25 times faster than the wider economy (AMVO).
  • Debit cards lead the online payment mix at 75 percent, credit at 49 percent, and cash channels such as Paynet and OxxoPay at 26 percent (AMVO).
  • The top five abandonment reasons AMVO records begin with shipping cost and include not feeling safe on the site and unclear return policies (AMVO).
  • Mexican law requires online sellers to publish a physical address and telephone number before the transaction (LFPC Art. 76 BIS fr. III).

What makes Mexican shoppers trust an online store?

Visible shipping cost, a site that feels legitimate, the payment method they actually use, and a clear return policy. AMVO records these among the top five reasons Mexican shoppers abandon a purchase, and a cross-border seller controls most of them.

The honest answer is that trust in Mexican e-commerce is less about badges and more about removing the specific frictions that make a shopper stop. AMVO, the Mexican online sales association, publishes the reasons buyers abandon a purchase, and their top five list is unusually useful because it is ordered rather than vague. The first is that shipping cost is too expensive. The second is not feeling safe on the site or the site not looking trustworthy. The third is not finding the product they were looking for. The fourth is the store not accepting the payment method they wanted. The fifth is that exchange and return policies are not clear. If you sell into Mexico from abroad, look at that list again: numbers one, two, four and five are all things you control, and they are precisely the places where a cross-border store tends to be weakest. AMVO groups the underlying causes into three buckets and the weights are worth knowing: information visibility and product research at 74 percent, problems in the purchase and payment process at 71 percent, and site and navigation problems at 61 percent. The market itself is not the constraint. Mexican e-commerce reached 941 billion pesos in 2025, growing 19.2 percent while the wider economy grew under one percent, with 77.2 million online buyers and 17.7 percent of all retail now online. The demand is there. What loses the sale is friction you can name and remove.

Get the payment mix right

Debit dominates at 75 percent, credit is 49 percent, and cash channels like OxxoPay and Paynet are still 26 percent. If you only accept international credit cards, you are invisible to a large share of Mexican buyers, including the newest ones entering e-commerce.

Payment is where most foreign sellers quietly lose Mexican customers, because the mix looks nothing like the United States. In AMVO's study of online buyers, debit cards lead at 75 percent and credit cards follow at 49 percent, which already inverts the assumption many US sellers bring with them. More striking is that cash channels, meaning services like Paynet and OxxoPay where the buyer completes the order online and pays in cash at a convenience store, still account for 26 percent. Bank transfer sits at 20 percent and cash on delivery at 15 percent. AMVO's own reading of this is important: cash usage went up rather than down, because lower-income and unbanked segments have been entering e-commerce, and those are exactly the buyers a growing store wants. The trend in the following year's data shows debit easing and credit rising, so the mix moves, but the headline holds: a checkout that only accepts international credit cards is closed to a large part of the market. Interest-free installments, known locally as meses sin intereses, are also a normal expectation in Mexican retail rather than a promotion, particularly above certain price points. Be careful with the numbers circulating about installments, because much of what gets quoted mixes several financial benefits together. What is documented is that Amazon Mexico announced in February 2026 that installments are offered on items above 299 MXN without adding a fee for the seller. The practical takeaway is simple: before optimising your product page, check whether a Mexican buyer can actually pay you the way they normally pay.

What the law requires you to show

Mexican consumer law requires you to publish a physical address and phone number before the transaction, give a minimum 60 day warranty, and honour a five business day cancellation window. If your address is abroad, the buyer cannot even take a complaint to PROFECO.

Beyond what shoppers prefer, Mexican law sets requirements that double as trust signals, and cross-border sellers routinely miss them. Article 76 BIS of the consumer protection law, which covers transactions in electronic media, obliges the seller to provide a physical address and telephone numbers before the transaction, along with full information about terms, conditions, costs and any additional charges. Article 77 sets a minimum warranty of 60 days from delivery, and it is worth correcting a widely repeated error here: the figure is 60 days, not 90. Article 56 gives the consumer five business days to revoke consent without liability, which PROFECO applies to online purchases in its own guidance. Article 92 BIS sets compensation at no less than 20 percent of the amount paid when a service is not delivered or is defective, and Article 53 puts the cost of shipping for warranty repairs or returns on the seller unless agreed otherwise. Then there is the point that matters most for a foreign seller, and it is a regulatory fact rather than a survey: PROFECO states that when the seller's address is outside the country, the consumer has to go to the international econsumer.gov platform instead of PROFECO. In other words, a store with no Mexican address is pushing its buyers outside Mexican consumer protection, and Mexican buyers understand this intuitively even if they never read the statute. That is the real argument for a local address and a local return point. It is not a badge on your footer, it is the difference between a buyer who has recourse and one who does not. BringGo Ship operates warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey, which is what makes a genuine Mexican address and a domestic return point possible for a seller based abroad.

Credit card49%Rising in later data
Cash (Paynet, OxxoPay)26%Grew, not shrank
Bank transfer20%Still common
Cash on delivery15%Trust-driven
BNPL (no card)7%Emerging

Definitions

  • AMVO: AMVO is the Mexican online sales association whose annual study is the primary source for Mexican e-commerce behaviour data.
  • OxxoPay / Paynet: OxxoPay and Paynet let a buyer order online and pay in cash at a convenience store, which is how a quarter of Mexican online purchases are settled.
  • Meses sin intereses: Meses sin intereses are interest-free instalments, a normal expectation in Mexican retail rather than a promotional extra.

Frequently asked questions

What makes Mexican shoppers trust an online store?

Visible shipping cost, a site that feels legitimate, the payment method they actually use, and a clear return policy. AMVO records these among the top five reasons Mexican shoppers abandon a purchase. If you sell from abroad, four of those five are things you control and they are where cross-border stores are usually weakest.

How do Mexicans pay online?

Debit cards lead at 75 percent, credit cards follow at 49 percent, and cash channels such as Paynet and OxxoPay still account for 26 percent, with bank transfer at 20 percent and cash on delivery at 15 percent. A checkout that only accepts international credit cards is closed to a large share of the market.

How big is Mexican e-commerce?

It reached 941 billion pesos in 2025, growing 19.2 percent year over year while the wider economy grew under one percent. There are 77.2 million online buyers and online now represents 17.7 percent of all Mexican retail, which places Mexico eighth in the world by market size.

What does Mexican law require an online seller to publish?

Article 76 BIS of the consumer protection law requires a physical address and telephone numbers before the transaction, plus full information on terms, costs and additional charges. Article 77 sets a minimum 60 day warranty from delivery, and Article 56 gives a five business day window to cancel without liability.

Why does a Mexican address matter for trust?

Because of jurisdiction. PROFECO states that when the seller's address is outside the country, the consumer must go to the international econsumer.gov platform instead of PROFECO. A store with no Mexican address pushes its buyers outside Mexican consumer protection, which is a concrete disadvantage rather than a matter of perception.

translations.title: USMCA Certificate Of Origin: How To Fill It Out Correctly
translations.excerpt: USMCA has no official certificate form, which confuses more importers than any other rule. What matters is nine data elements, and getting them right is worth real money.
translations.content:
There is no official USMCA certificate of origin form. The certification only needs to contain nine required data elements and can appear on a commercial invoice or any other document. The exporter, producer or importer may certify. A blanket certification covers up to 12 months of shipments, the document is accepted for four years, and records must be kept for five.

  • USMCA prescribes no form; CBP Form 434 is no longer in use and NAFTA paperwork is not valid for USMCA claims (CBP).
  • The certification must contain the nine minimum data elements set out in USMCA Annex 5-A (USTR).
  • The exporter, the producer or the importer may complete it, and no Party can force a producer or exporter to issue one (USMCA Art. 5.2, 5.3.4).
  • A blanket certification covers multiple shipments of identical goods for a period of up to 12 months (Art. 5.3.5).
  • The certification is accepted for four years from the date it was signed, and records must be kept for five years (Art. 5.3.6, 5.8).

How do I complete a USMCA certificate of origin?

By including nine specific data elements on any document you choose, including a commercial invoice. There is no official form to download. The one hard restriction is that the certification cannot be issued on an invoice from a country outside the agreement.

The first thing to understand is that the document most people go looking for does not exist. USMCA deliberately prescribes no format: the agreement says the certification need not follow a prescribed format, that it may be provided on an invoice or any other document, and that it simply has to describe the goods in enough detail to identify them. CBP has confirmed that the old NAFTA form, CBP Form 434, is no longer in use, and that even if the origin rule and all the data happen to be the same, goods must be certified again under USMCA rather than relying on NAFTA paperwork. What the agreement does require is nine data elements, listed in Annex 5-A. One, state whether the certifier is the importer, exporter or producer. Two, the certifier's name, title, address including country, telephone and email. Three, the exporter's details if different from the certifier, with an address in the Party country from which the good is exported. Four, the producer's details if different, with the option to write Various when there are several, or to state that the information is available on request from the importing authorities. Five, the importer's details if known. Six, a description of the good and its HS tariff classification at the six digit level, plus the export invoice number if the certification covers a single shipment. Seven, the origin criterion under which the good qualifies. Eight, the blanket period if it covers multiple shipments. Nine, the authorised signature and date, together with the certification statement given in the annex. There is one restriction that catches people out: the certification cannot be issued on an invoice or commercial document issued in a non-Party country. If your invoice comes from outside the region, put the certification on a separate document.

Who can certify, and for how long?

The exporter, the producer or the importer, which is the biggest change from NAFTA. A blanket certification covers up to 12 months of identical goods, the document itself is accepted for four years, and you must keep supporting records for five years.

Under USMCA any of three parties can issue the certification, and this is the most useful change from the NAFTA era. A producer certifies on the basis of its own information showing the good originates. An exporter that is not the producer certifies either on its own information or by reasonably relying on the producer's written representation. An importer certifies only on the basis of its own information and documents, which means an importer cannot simply lean on the exporter's word, and cannot later make a second claim for the same import based on an exporter or producer certification. It is also worth knowing that no country can compel a producer or exporter to issue a certification at all, so if a supplier refuses, the importer route may be the only path. Three time periods matter and they are routinely confused with each other. The blanket period is how many shipments one document covers: up to 12 months of identical goods, meaning goods that are the same in all respects including physical characteristics, quality and reputation, where minor differences in appearance do not matter. The validity period is how long the document is accepted by customs: four years from the date it was signed. The recordkeeping period is how long you keep the evidence behind it: at least five years, running from the date of importation for the importer and from the date the certification was issued for the exporter or producer. That last obligation applies even if the importing country never asks for the certification or waives it entirely.

The rules that save you money and mistakes

Small errors cannot be grounds for rejection, you get at least five business days to fix a defective certification, and you can claim preference up to a year after importation. Below a value threshold no certification is needed at all, but confirm the Mexican figure with your broker.

Several provisions exist specifically to stop good faith mistakes from costing you duty, and few importers use them. Customs cannot reject a certification because of minor errors or discrepancies that do not put the accuracy of the import documents in doubt. If a certification is illegible or defective, the importer must be given at least five business days to provide a corrected one, so a rejected entry is usually recoverable rather than lost. If you did not claim preferential treatment at the time of import, you can still claim a refund for up to one year after the date of importation, which is the single most overlooked way to recover money already paid. If you discover your own certification was wrong, correcting the document and paying the duty promptly protects you from penalties, and the same protection exists for an exporter or producer who notifies the error in writing. The certification may be written in English, French or Spanish, and electronic issuance and electronic or digital signatures must be accepted, so there is no need to chase wet signatures. On low value shipments the agreement sets a baseline: no certification is required where the value of the importation does not exceed 1,000 US dollars, or a higher amount set by the importing country, provided the shipment is not part of a series arranged to avoid the rules. The United States applies 2,500 dollars on its side. We could not verify Mexico's own figure from an official Mexican source, so treat 1,000 dollars as the agreement floor and confirm the current Mexican threshold with your customs broker before relying on it. Finally, the 2026 joint review has not changed any of this. The United States did not agree to renew the agreement in its current form, but USTR confirmed the agreement remains in force pending resolution, so preferential tariffs, origin rules and every procedure above apply as normal today. BringGo Ship prepares origin documentation as part of clearance, so US origin goods move duty free instead of paying a tariff they never owed.

USMCA certification: the periods that get confused

PeriodHow longWhat it means
Blanket periodUp to 12 monthsHow many shipments one document covers
Validity4 yearsHow long customs accepts the document
Recordkeeping5 yearsHow long you keep supporting evidence
Post-import claim1 yearWindow to claim a refund after import
Fix a defectAt least 5 business daysTime to supply a corrected certification
Certification threshold1,000 USD baselineUS applies 2,500; verify Mexico

Definitions

  • Certification of origin: A certification of origin is the statement, in any format, that a good qualifies as originating under USMCA and contains the nine required data elements.
  • Blanket period: A blanket period lets one certification cover multiple shipments of identical goods for up to 12 months.
  • Identical goods: Identical goods are the same in all respects including physical characteristics, quality and reputation, where minor appearance differences do not matter.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an official USMCA certificate of origin form?

No. USMCA prescribes no format. The certification only needs to contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A and can be placed on a commercial invoice or any other document. CBP Form 434 from the NAFTA era is no longer in use, and NAFTA paperwork cannot be relied on for a USMCA claim even when the origin rule is the same.

Who can complete a USMCA certification of origin?

The exporter, the producer or the importer. That third option is the main change from NAFTA. An importer must certify on the basis of its own information rather than the exporter's word. No country can force a producer or exporter to issue one, so if a supplier refuses, certifying as the importer may be the only route available.

How long is a USMCA certification valid?

Customs accepts it for four years from the date it was signed. This is different from the blanket period, which is how many shipments one document covers and is capped at 12 months, and different again from recordkeeping, which is five years. Confusing these three is one of the most common compliance errors.

Can I claim USMCA preference after the goods have already been imported?

Yes. If preferential treatment was not claimed at the time of import, you can apply for a refund for up to one year after the date of importation. This is the most overlooked way to recover duty already paid, and it is worth reviewing past entries where origin documentation existed but was never used.

Do small shipments need a certificate of origin?

The agreement sets a baseline of 1,000 US dollars, below which no certification is required, provided the shipment is not part of a series arranged to avoid the rules. The United States applies 2,500 dollars on its side. Mexico's own threshold should be confirmed with your customs broker before you rely on it.

  • US Customs and Border Protection, USMCA FAQs (cbp.gov)
  • SAT (Mexican tax administration) (sat.gob.mx)

translations.title: Shipping Supplements And Vitamins To Mexico: The Hard Truth
translations.excerpt: Supplements do not need product registration in Mexico, which is why so many sellers assume they are unregulated. They still need an import permit, and health claims will get them seized.
translations.content:
Supplements do not require a product registration in Mexico, but they do require a prior sanitary import permit obtained through the VUCEM window, an importing business registered by notice of operation, a Spanish label carrying two mandatory phrases, and ingredients within Mexico's maximum daily doses. Any therapeutic or health claim reclassifies the product as a medicine and stops the shipment.

  • Supplements are not on the list of products requiring registro sanitario under the General Health Law, Article 376 (LGS).
  • They do require a prior sanitary import permit, filed through the VUCEM single window and attached to the pedimento (Secretaría de Salud import regulation).
  • The importing business must file an Aviso de Funcionamiento at least 30 days before starting activity (LGS Art. 200 Bis).
  • NOM-051 does not apply to supplements; the binding labelling rules are in the health products regulation, Appendix XVII (COFEPRIS).
  • In February 2026 COFEPRIS issued an alert against a US supplement brand, citing English labelling, health claims and a missing import permit.

Can I sell US supplements in Mexico?

Yes, but not the way most sellers assume. There is no product registration, which is why people think supplements are lightly regulated. What there is instead is a prior import permit, a registered Mexican importer and strict labelling rules, and skipping any of them stops the goods.

The confusion around supplements in Mexico comes from one true fact that gets misread. It is true that supplements do not require a registro sanitario, the product registration that medicines and medical devices need, because Article 376 of the General Health Law lists what needs registration and supplements are not on it. COFEPRIS says the same thing plainly: what supplement makers file is a notice of operation, which does not constitute any kind of authorisation or registration. Many sellers stop reading there and conclude that supplements are effectively unregulated. That conclusion is wrong and expensive. Registration of the product and permission to import the product are two different things, and supplements need the second one. They sit inside the annex of goods whose import is regulated by the health ministry, which means a prior sanitary import permit is mandatory, obtained through the VUCEM single window and attached to the pedimento as an electronic document. In practice a shipment without that permit does not clear. There is a second requirement people miss: the importing business, not the product, must file an Aviso de Funcionamiento with the health authority at least 30 days before it starts operating, and that filing has to name the party responsible. As of August 2025 the permit process was simplified into a single procedure with a four day resolution time instead of five, and the old requirement to submit an original origin label was dropped. So the honest summary is this: you do not register your product, you register your operation and you license each import.

The labelling rules are not the ones you expect

NOM-051, the food labelling standard everyone cites, does not apply to supplements. The binding rules sit in Appendix XVII of the health products regulation, and they require two specific phrases in capitals and bold, plus a full Spanish label before the product is sold.

This is where most published advice about Mexican supplements is simply wrong. Commercial blogs routinely tell sellers to comply with NOM-051, the front of pack food labelling standard, but COFEPRIS states in its own legal framework page that NOM-051 does not apply to supplements, and the economy ministry's application criterion says the same. What actually binds is Appendix XVII of the health products regulation, and it is specific. The label must carry the generic and specific product name, a full ingredient list in order of quantity, and where the product contains plants, both the common name and the botanical name at genus and species level. It must state any component that could pose a health risk, a nutritional declaration, the name and address of the manufacturer or importer, packer and distributor, instructions for storage, preparation and consumption, the lot number and the expiry date. Then there are two phrases that must appear together, in capital letters, in bold and in a contrasting colour, at the same point size as the rest of the information panel, with a clear space around them of at least one letter height. The first is that this product is not a medicine. The second is that consumption of this product is the responsibility of whoever recommends it and whoever uses it. Minimum letter height is set by the area of the information panel, starting at half a millimetre for very small panels and rising to three millimetres for panels above 161 square centimetres. And the label must be in Spanish before the product is offered for sale, not after it arrives. For imported goods packaged at origin, the regulation is explicit that the Spanish information has to be there prior to commercialisation, which is why labelling at origin is almost always cheaper than relabelling in Mexico.

Health claims and banned ingredients are what actually gets you seized

Mexico bans therapeutic claims outright, and a claim can reclassify your supplement as a medicine. Specific substances are prohibited, and vitamins and minerals have hard maximum daily doses. A February 2026 COFEPRIS alert against a US brand hit all of these at once.

The rules that most often stop a shipment are not paperwork rules, they are content rules. On ingredients, the regulation names substances that supplements must not contain: procaine, ephedrine, yohimbine, germanium, animal or human hormones, plants that are not permitted for infusions or teas, and any recognised pharmacological substance or anything representing a health risk. If your product contains a little known substance that could pose a risk, both its processing and its import depend on proving harmlessness scientifically to COFEPRIS first. Vitamins and minerals carry hard maximum daily doses, and exceeding them can push a product out of the supplement category altogether. Vitamin A is capped at 1000 micrograms, vitamin C at 300 milligrams, vitamin D at 10 micrograms, vitamin E at 200 milligrams, iron at 20 milligrams, zinc at 20 milligrams and calcium at 1200 milligrams, among others. On claims, the position is stricter than most US sellers expect. The regulation prohibits labelling or advertising that confuses, exaggerates or misleads, and specifically prohibits showing any preventive, rehabilitative or therapeutic indication. Labels cannot reference a disease, symptom, syndrome, anatomical feature or physiological process, and cannot claim the product replaces a meal or covers nutritional needs on its own. Brand names themselves cannot contain such references. If the authority attributes a therapeutic property to your product, it is legally treated as a medicine, which means it cannot be sold without meeting medicine rules. This is not theoretical. In February 2026 COFEPRIS issued a health alert against a US supplement brand sold through e-commerce platforms and apps, citing therapeutic claims such as restoring mental clarity and supporting healthy immune function, an English language label, prohibited plant ingredients, and the absence of both product registration and an import permit. The alert stated the products must not be distributed by any route, expressly including national and international courier and parcel services. One more change worth noting: a reform published in January 2026 added supplements explicitly to the article of the General Health Law covering sanitary control of processing, import and export, which puts the category on firmer statutory ground rather than changing the day to day rules. BringGo Ship works with a licensed Mexican customs broker, so permit filing and Spanish labelling happen before the goods move rather than after they are held.

Supplements into Mexico: what is and is not required

RequirementNeeded?Note
Product registration (registro sanitario)NoNot listed in LGS Art. 376
Prior sanitary import permitYesVia VUCEM, attached to pedimento
Aviso de Funcionamiento (the business)YesAt least 30 days before activity
NOM-051 food labellingNoDoes not apply to supplements
Spanish label, Appendix XVIIYesBefore commercialisation
Two mandatory phrasesYesCapitals, bold, contrasting
Health or therapeutic claimsProhibitedReclassifies product as medicine

Definitions

  • Registro sanitario: Registro sanitario is Mexican product registration required for medicines and certain devices, and it is not required for supplements.
  • Permiso sanitario de importación: The prior sanitary import permit is the licence each supplement import needs, filed through VUCEM and attached to the pedimento.
  • Aviso de Funcionamiento: The Aviso de Funcionamiento is the notice a Mexican business files at least 30 days before starting activity, and it is a notification rather than an approval.

Frequently asked questions

Do supplements need registration to be sold in Mexico?

No product registration is required, because supplements are not on the list in Article 376 of the General Health Law. But this is where most sellers go wrong: registration and import permission are different things. Supplements do require a prior sanitary import permit for each import, filed through VUCEM and attached to the customs declaration.

Does NOM-051 apply to supplements in Mexico?

No. COFEPRIS states in its own legal framework that NOM-051 does not apply to supplements, and the economy ministry's application criterion agrees. Much commercial advice online says otherwise and is wrong. The binding labelling rules are in Appendix XVII of the health products regulation, which sets different and more specific requirements.

What must a Mexican supplement label say?

The product name, full ingredient list in order of quantity with botanical names for plants, risk components, nutritional declaration, importer name and address, storage and use instructions, lot number and expiry date. Two phrases are mandatory in capitals and bold: that the product is not a medicine, and that consumption is the responsibility of whoever recommends and uses it.

Can I make health claims on supplements in Mexico?

No. The regulation prohibits any preventive, rehabilitative or therapeutic indication, and bans references to diseases, symptoms, syndromes or physiological processes on the label or in the brand name. If the authority attributes a therapeutic property to your product it is legally treated as a medicine and cannot be sold as a supplement.

Which ingredients are banned in Mexican supplements?

The regulation names procaine, ephedrine, yohimbine, germanium, animal or human hormones, plants not permitted for teas and infusions, and any recognised pharmacological substance or health risk. Vitamins and minerals also carry maximum daily doses, for example 1000 micrograms of vitamin A and 300 milligrams of vitamin C, and exceeding them can push the product out of the supplement category.
